reasoning:
Country-level: The scene shows right-hand traffic, EU-style road furniture, and multiple distinctly German elements: EU license plates with the “D” country identifier and long hyphenated format; red–white diagonal hazard bollards; German-style speed-limit sign with a white background and red ring; the blue mandatory-direction sign; and curved mast traffic signals common in Germany. These collectively rule out non-EU countries and strongly indicate Germany over neighboring countries due to the plate font/format and signage set.
City-level: Dense, prewar-to-midcentury plastered apartment blocks 5–6 stories tall, narrow carriageway with inset curbs, and tree-lined side streets suggest a large southern German city. The specific signal heads on swept-back poles and the prevalence of such urban blocks match Munich more than Berlin (which has wider avenues and different light masts) or Hamburg (more brick). While the visible passenger car plate “PM-…” is from Potsdam-Mittelmark, cars can travel; it does not fix location. The overall architecture and traffic-light hardware are typical for Munich neighborhoods outside the center.
Street-level: A 30 km/h zone sign at the intersection, a small splitter island with a blue ‘keep right’ bollard, and painted lane arrows indicating one lane ahead and a dedicated right-turn lane characterize a residential-arterial junction. The presence of a no-entry sign on the left suggests a one-way side street. The arrangement of dual signal heads for the right-turn lane and straight-through lane, plus the narrow median and specific curb geometry, narrows to a local Munich neighborhood street rather than a major boulevard.
Overall, the strongest reliable conclusion is Germany; the city inference to Munich is plausible but less certain.

features.geolocation_description: EU-format license plates with the blue band and German ‘D’ identifier and hyphenated district code strongly indicate Germany.
Red–white diagonal hazard bollards and chevron markers are standard German street furniture.
German-style circular 30 km/h sign and accompanying ‘Zone’ style indicate German traffic sign conventions.
Curved mast traffic lights with compact three-aspect heads are common in many German cities, including Munich.
Blue mandatory-direction sign (straight or right) follows German StVO iconography and mounting.
Architecture: 5–6 story stuccoed apartment blocks with bay windows and modest ornamentation typical of southern German cities such as Munich.
Lane markings: one through lane with a separate right-turn lane and arrows, plus a small splitter island and ‘keep right’ bollard—details that help pinpoint the exact junction geometry.
No-entry sign on the left indicates a one-way side street feeding into the junction, helping to distinguish this intersection layout.
